passages.text: Dyspnea during exercise and voluntary hyperpnea in women with obesity

Temporal responses of ratings of perceived breathlessness (RBP) during constant-load and incremental exercise, and during voluntary hyperpnea (EVH) were examined in obese women. Following 6min of constant-load (60W) cycling, 34 women rated RPB≥4 (+DOE) and 22 women rated RPB≤2 (−DOE). Introduction

Obesity is associated with numerous health problems and exerts limitations to breathing capacity including decreased pulmonary function and altered respiratory mechanics. These effects could provoke dyspnea on exertion (−DOE), which is a very common symptom in obesity. However, not all individuals with obesity appear to experience DOE. At present, it remains unclear as to what mechanism(s) underlie the different ratings of perceived breathlessness (RPB; an indicator of DOE) in women with obesity. Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to explore the dynamic response of RBP during constant-load and incremental exercise, as well as at various levels of eucapnic voluntary hyperpnea (EVH). Methods

The data presented in this article were collected as part of a larger study describing the effects of weight loss on pulmonary function and breathing mechanics during exercise in women with obesity. However, the current article addresses a different question, and we repeat only the methods and data (i.e., subject characteristics, peak exercise data, and dyspnea ratings during exercise and EVH) ess
Participants:

In total, 78 women with obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥30 and ≤45) were retrospectively examined. Participants were eligible to participate if they did not have a history of smoking, asthma, cardiovascular disease, sleep disorders, or musculoskeletal abnormalities that would preclude exercise. Study design:

Participants visited the laboratory on three separate occasions. On the first visit, participants underwent initial screening, standard anthropometric and body composition measures, and pulmonary function testing (data not shown). On the second visit, participants completed submaximal constant-load and maximal incremental cycling tests, and on the third visit participants completed EVH testing.
